text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: A pharmaceutical company finishes a big clinical trial. Years of work, thousands of patients, a huge pile of data. The results look good. What happens next?

speaker: JAMES
text: Most people would say: the medicine gets approved and doctors start prescribing it. But in between there's an enormous amount of writing. The trial has to be published in a medical journal. The results have to be presented at conferences. Doctors need clear, accurate educational material. Health systems and insurers want evidence that the medicine is worth paying for.

speaker: NORA
text: And all of it has to be scientifically precise, fair and balanced, and checked by medical, legal and regulatory reviewers before it goes anywhere.

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot of that work is done by specialist agencies, staffed by people with doctorates in science and medicine. Today's company is one of them. And it's a business where generative AI, which is very good at producing words, meets a world where every word has to be right.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills, which we'll often call LLCP. Today it's Prime Global, a medical communications and market access group headquartered in Knutsford, in the north-west of England.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: the company's own pages, the private equity firm's announcements, trade press and adviser releases. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a figure comes from the company, we'll flag it. And because we'll be talking about medicines and clinical evidence, a clear reminder: nothing here is medical advice, and nothing here is investment advice either.

speaker: JAMES
text: And one quick clarification for anyone searching online. There's a completely different business called PrimeGlobal, an accountancy network in the United States. Not the same company. We're talking about Prime Global the medical communications group.

speaker: NORA
text: Good. So the one-sentence version. What is Prime Global?

speaker: JAMES
text: Prime Global helps pharmaceutical and other life-science companies communicate the science behind their medicines, to doctors, to payers and to patients. It does scientific publications, medical strategy, health economics and market access work, commercial launch support and patient engagement.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because in October 2025 it appointed a senior leader whose title literally includes AI: Global Executive Vice President for Medical Communications, AI and Digital Healthcare. And it has launched an in-house hub it calls Prime Solutions Lab, which it says uses AI for insights and predictive modelling. So the company is clearly leaning into AI. The question is how AI changes a business built on highly skilled people writing very carefully.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is it, and how big?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's headquartered in Knutsford, in Cheshire, with other UK bases in London and Macclesfield. The Macclesfield office opened in November 2016. The legal entity is Prime Global Medical Communications Limited. It was founded in 1997, so it's nearly thirty years old. And through acquisitions it now has people in the United States, Europe and New Zealand as well.

speaker: NORA
text: Headcount? Revenue?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's where it gets thin. The latest figures we found are old. In 2016 it had over one hundred employees. After it bought Cambridge Medical Communication, around 2020, a report said the combined workforce was more than two hundred and sixty. Since then, it has made three more acquisitions, so today it is presumably larger, but we didn't find a current headcount, revenue or client count. The homepage talks about decades of experience and has a testimonial, but no numbers.

speaker: NORA
text: What does it say about its people?

speaker: JAMES
text: One striking claim. It says eighty percent of its scientific and editorial staff hold a PhD, an MD or a PharmD, which is a doctorate in pharmacy. That's a company figure, but it tells you what kind of business this is. It sells scientific expertise. The writers are scientists.

speaker: NORA
text: Why does that matter so much to clients?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because, in general, the people reading and approving the work at a pharma company are themselves scientists and doctors. If an agency writer doesn't understand the biology, the statistics or the clinical context, it shows quickly, and the client has to do the thinking themselves. A writer with a doctorate in the relevant field can engage as a peer, challenge a weak argument and spot an error in the data. That's what clients pay a premium for.

speaker: NORA
text: And it makes the team expensive.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does. Highly qualified people command good salaries, and they're in demand across the industry. So the business has a high-quality, high-cost workforce. That's a theme that runs through the whole AI discussion: how do you get more out of your most expensive and most valuable people?

speaker: NORA
text: And who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Graeme Peterson is chair and group chief executive, as of October 2025, and was described as founder and chief executive in 2022. Valerie Moss is chief scientific officer. Brian Norman is named as chief technology officer, although that comes from an undated social media post. James Karcher joined in October 2025 as the global executive vice president for medical communications, AI and digital healthcare. And there are other senior names, like David Hogben, who leads omnichannel strategy and delivery, and Megan Pollack, a vice president at Prime Aventine, the US business.

speaker: NORA
text: Founder-led, still.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, nearly thirty years in, the founder is still at the helm. That's quite common in agency businesses, and it usually means a strong culture and deep client relationships. It also raises the usual questions about succession, which any long-term owner will think about.

speaker: NORA
text: What does it call its customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Life-science companies, which in practice means pharmaceutical and biotech firms. We didn't find named clients, which is normal in this sector, because pharma clients are often confidential about which agencies they use.

speaker: NORA
text: Now the ownership and deals.

speaker: JAMES
text: Before LLCP, Prime was owned by its founders and shareholders, who aren't named in the sources. In April 2021, LLCP invested from its European fund, and it still holds the company. The deal value wasn't disclosed. BDO and the law firm Addleshaw Goddard advised Prime and its shareholders.

speaker: NORA
text: So about five and a half years.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, from April 2021 to now. In private equity terms, that's a mature hold. So, our inference, the next couple of years matter a lot for how the company's story is told to any future owner.

speaker: NORA
text: And the acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four that we found. The first, Cambridge Medical Communication, was announced in May 2020, which is before LLCP arrived, so it's not an LLCP deal. Then under LLCP: in January 2022, HCD Economics, which does health economics and burden-of-disease research. In September 2022, earthware, a digital healthcare agency. And in December 2023, Aventine Consulting, which does US market access and payer communications, with bases in Boston and Seattle. Terms were undisclosed for all of them.

speaker: NORA
text: Talk me through the logic of those three.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a neat set, in my view. HCD Economics adds the ability to show what a disease costs and what a medicine is worth, which is the language of health systems and insurers. earthware adds digital capability, building tools and channels rather than just documents. And Aventine adds a US foothold in payer communications, which is crucial because the United States is the largest pharmaceutical market and its insurers demand detailed evidence.

speaker: NORA
text: So, science, economics, digital and the US.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the shape. Each deal fills a gap in the lifecycle of a medicine. And notice what's missing since December 2023: no acquisitions, no funding news, no product launches, in the last two years that we could find. The news has been about people, the AI leadership hire, and thought leadership.

speaker: NORA
text: Is that a slowdown?

speaker: JAMES
text: It could be. Or it could be a period of integration and organic growth after a busy buying phase. From the outside, we can't tell. I'd just note it as a quieter period.

speaker: NORA
text: I suspect a lot of listeners have never heard of medical communications as an industry. Give us the primer.

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure, as general background. Pharmaceutical companies have to communicate about their medicines in tightly controlled ways. There's a broad split, in general terms, between medical affairs, which is about sharing scientific information in a balanced, non-promotional way, and commercial, which is about promotion within strict rules. Medical communications agencies work on both sides, but the science is at the core.

speaker: NORA
text: What does the work look like?

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot of it is publications. When a trial finishes, the results need to be written up for a peer-reviewed journal, and presented as abstracts and posters at medical congresses. Agencies help plan which publications to produce, when and where, and medical writers help the researchers draft them, following ethical guidelines on authorship and transparency.

speaker: NORA
text: And beyond publications?

speaker: JAMES
text: Slide kits for medical teams to present data. Training for pharmaceutical company staff who talk to doctors. Educational programmes. Advisory boards, where companies hear from experts. Materials for patients. And increasingly, digital content, websites, apps, interactive tools.

speaker: NORA
text: Why do pharma companies hire agencies for this? Couldn't they write it themselves?

speaker: JAMES
text: Some do some of it. But in general, there are a few reasons to outsource. Workload is lumpy: a big trial readout or a launch creates a surge of work, and it's cheaper to bring in an agency than to staff for the peak. Expertise is specialised: writing a publication to journal standards, or building a health economic model, takes skills a company may not need full-time. And agencies see many companies and many therapy areas, so they bring experience of what works.

speaker: NORA
text: And there are ethical rules around all this, I assume.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and they matter. Speaking generally, publication guidelines in the industry set out that authors must be the people who genuinely contributed to the research and the paper, and that professional writing support should be disclosed. The aim is transparency: readers should know who did what and who paid for it. Good agencies take those rules very seriously, because their reputation, and their clients', depends on it.

speaker: NORA
text: So the writer is a support act, not the author.

speaker: JAMES
text: In publications, typically, yes. The writer helps the authors communicate clearly and accurately. That's a useful frame for thinking about AI too. If an AI helps the writer, that's another layer of support, and the same questions about disclosure and responsibility apply.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned MLR earlier. What is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Medical, legal and regulatory review. In general, before any material goes out, it's reviewed by the pharma company's medical, legal and regulatory teams to make sure it's accurate, balanced, properly referenced and compliant with the rules. That review is thorough and often slow. Every claim must be supported by a reference. That's a crucial fact for the AI story, because it means speed in drafting doesn't automatically mean speed to market.

speaker: NORA
text: And market access?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's about getting a medicine paid for. A regulator might approve a medicine as safe and effective, but then a health system or an insurer decides whether to cover it and at what price. They want evidence of value: how much the disease costs, how the medicine changes outcomes, how it compares with alternatives. That's where health economics and outcomes research, shortened to HEOR, comes in, along with real-world evidence, meaning data from actual clinical practice rather than trials.

speaker: NORA
text: So Prime covers the journey from the lab results all the way to the insurer.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's its pitch. Its own five service lines are strategic consultancy and lifecycle management; medical strategy, publications and scientific communications; HEOR, real-world evidence and market access; commercial launch and promotional education; and patient engagement and insights.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go a bit deeper on how those service lines fit together.

speaker: JAMES
text: Think about a medicine's life. Years before launch, strategic consultancy helps a company plan: what are the unmet needs, who are the key audiences, what evidence will they need? As trial data arrives, the publications and scientific communications team helps get it into journals and congresses. Around approval, the market access team, supported by health economics, builds the value case for payers. At launch, the commercial team supports promotional education. And throughout, patient engagement helps understand and communicate with the people taking the medicine.

speaker: NORA
text: So one client could use all five.

speaker: JAMES
text: In principle, yes, and that's the strategic logic of having them all. A client that uses Prime for publications might also use it for market access, and so on. That's cross-selling, and in agency businesses it's a big part of growth.

speaker: NORA
text: And Prime Solutions Lab, where does that fit?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's described as a blended hub of creatives, technologists, strategists and scientists, recently launched, though the page is undated. It says it uses AI to, quote, distil complex data, and cites predictive modelling and AI capabilities. It doesn't name a specific product. So I'd see it as a team that brings technology and AI into client work, across the service lines, rather than a product you can buy off the shelf.

speaker: NORA
text: And earthware?

speaker: JAMES
text: earthware was a digital healthcare agency, so it brings the ability to build digital tools. In my view, it's a natural partner for the omnichannel work David Hogben leads. Omnichannel, in this context, means reaching doctors and patients consistently through many channels: email, websites, events, sales representatives, and so on. And the AI leader's remit, according to the announcement, covers AI-enabled communications and advanced analytics.

speaker: NORA
text: How does Prime get paid?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have Prime's specific terms, so this is general to the sector. Agencies are usually paid by project or through retainers, and the price is largely driven by the time of skilled people. A publication, a slide kit, an advisory board each has a fee that reflects the hours involved. Which, as we'll see, is exactly why AI is both an opportunity and a threat.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Walk me through one piece of work, invented.

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. A made-up mid-sized biotech, let's call it Northbrook Therapeutics, has just finished a phase three trial of a new medicine for a chronic lung condition. It hires an agency like Prime to support the primary publication in a medical journal, plus an abstract and poster for a major respiratory congress in six months.

speaker: NORA
text: Who's involved?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the agency side, a medical writer with a doctorate in respiratory science, an editor, a project manager and an account lead. On the client side, the medical affairs team, the clinical team who ran the trial, and of course the academic investigators who will be the authors. Under good publication practice, the authors are the scientists who did the work; the writer supports them.

speaker: NORA
text: And the work?

speaker: JAMES
text: The writer starts with the clinical study report, which is a very long document, plus the statistical tables. She reads it all, and builds an outline with the authors: the key findings, the story, the structure. Then she drafts the manuscript: introduction, methods, results, discussion. Every number must match the source tables. Every statement in the discussion must be supported by references.

speaker: NORA
text: How long does that take?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, weeks of skilled time, and then rounds of review. Authors comment. The client's medical team comments. MLR reviews. The writer revises. Several cycles. Then submission to the journal, peer review, more revisions. And in parallel, the abstract and poster for the congress, which need the same accuracy in fewer words.

speaker: NORA
text: Where does the time go?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, a lot of it goes on tasks that are skilled but not the highest-value part of the job. Reading and summarising long documents. Checking that every number matches. Formatting references. Turning the full paper into a shorter abstract and then into a poster. Reconciling comments from five reviewers who disagree. The truly expert work, framing the story honestly and getting the science right, is a smaller share of the hours than you might think.

speaker: NORA
text: So that's where AI could help.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the hypothesis. Not to replace the writer's judgment, but to take some of the reading, summarising, checking and reformatting off her plate. And we'll come back to how that might look.

speaker: NORA
text: And what happens to the doctor at the end of the chain?

speaker: JAMES
text: A respiratory specialist reads the paper in the journal, sees the poster at the congress, and gets a clear, accurate picture of what the trial showed, benefits and risks. That's the point of the whole exercise. Done well, it helps doctors make better decisions for their patients.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk market. How big is medical communications?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable number. One market research page puts a medical writing market at nearly two hundred billion dollars for 2026, but that seems implausibly large for medical writing services and looks mis-scoped, so we're not using it. Rather than give you a dubious number, I'll say: it's a sizeable, specialised services market, and we don't have a trustworthy figure.

speaker: NORA
text: What do buyers want?

speaker: JAMES
text: A 2023 analysis by L.E.K. Consulting said that biopharma companies are increasingly outsourcing commercial, marketing, medical affairs and market access work to communications providers, and are prioritising digital and quantitative skills. That fits Prime's moves into digital, through earthware, and health economics, through HCD.

speaker: NORA
text: And demand drivers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Outsourcing is one. Omnichannel engagement with doctors and patients is another. The need for evidence for US payers, which is why the Aventine deal makes sense. And the need for health economic evidence more broadly, which is HCD's area. We didn't find a growth rate for the category.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: Competitor coverage in our research was thin, so I'll be careful. The one we verified is Six Degrees Medical, now part of Reverba, which has headquarters in Toronto and teams in the UK, and does medical writing, publication planning and digital. Reverba bought it in April 2024. Then there are names that came up in our research but that we didn't verify in detail: Fishawack and Envision Pharma Group. And from general industry knowledge, other established medical communications agencies include Ashfield, Adelphi and Costello Medical. We didn't check their current ownership or offers, so treat that as background.

speaker: NORA
text: And the big agency groups?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, the healthcare communications world includes some very large networks with big technology budgets. That matters for AI, because a bigger group can afford to build proprietary AI tools and spread the cost across many clients. A mid-sized independent like Prime has to be smarter about where it invests.

speaker: NORA
text: Any AI-native challengers?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find one in this space. But that doesn't mean there aren't any, or that there won't be. In other professional services, AI-native start-ups have appeared that promise faster, cheaper drafting. It seems likely that will happen in medical writing too, if it hasn't already.

speaker: NORA
text: How do pharma companies pick an agency?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, often through a formal selection process, sometimes called a pitch, and often for a specific product or therapy area. Big pharma companies may have a list of preferred agencies, and procurement teams negotiate rates. Relationships matter a lot: a medical affairs director who has worked well with an agency team tends to bring them back. And therapy area expertise is a big differentiator. An agency known for respiratory or oncology work has an edge in those areas.

speaker: NORA
text: And procurement teams will have views on AI.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd expect so. Our guess is that procurement teams will increasingly ask agencies how they use AI and what it means for price. If an agency says it uses AI but charges the same hours, procurement will push back. That's another reason to have a clear pricing story ready.

speaker: NORA
text: And the pharma companies themselves?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the other competitor, in a sense. If generative AI makes drafting much faster, some pharma companies may decide to do more of the work in-house with smaller teams and AI tools. That's an inference, but it's a real risk for any agency whose value is mainly hours of writing.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the reality check. Where is Prime with AI today?

speaker: JAMES
text: Here's the evidence. In October 2025, the creation of a global executive vice president role for medical communications, AI and digital healthcare, with James Karcher in post, and a remit that covers AI-enabled communications and advanced analytics. Prime Solutions Lab, which says it uses AI to distil complex data and cites predictive modelling. The chief scientific officer, Valerie Moss, co-leading a session on AI in medical communications at an industry academy run by ISMPP, the International Society for Medical Publication Professionals, though the year isn't stated. An undated social media post about the chief technology officer leading an internal session on small-scale AI applications. And the homepage claims award-winning creative, digital and AI solutions.

speaker: NORA
text: And what didn't you find?

speaker: JAMES
text: No named AI product or tool. No description of AI inside the core writing workflow. No AI partnerships. No published AI governance policy or security certifications. So the picture is a company with AI leadership in place, an internal hub, and clear interest, but no public evidence yet of AI embedded in how its core deliverables are produced.

speaker: NORA
text: How would you characterise that?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, Prime is ahead of many services firms on leadership and intent. Putting AI in a senior executive's title is a real commitment. It's at an earlier stage on process: making AI a normal part of how a publication or slide kit gets made, with measured results.

speaker: NORA
text: Why might it be cautious?

speaker: JAMES
text: Good reasons. First, accuracy. In medical communications, a hallucinated number or a made-up reference is not a typo, it's a serious problem. Second, confidentiality. Clinical trial data before publication is highly sensitive, and clients will want to know exactly where it goes. Third, client rules. Many pharma companies have their own policies on whether and how agencies can use AI on their work. And fourth, industry guidance on AI in publications is still evolving, including around disclosure of AI use.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's dig into the confidentiality point. What would a client want to know?

speaker: JAMES
text: Speaking generally, a pharma client sharing unpublished trial data with an agency would want to know a few things before allowing AI anywhere near it. Which AI tools are used, and are they enterprise versions with contractual protections? Where is the data processed and stored? Is any of it used to train models that others benefit from? Who at the agency can see it? And how is it deleted when the project ends? Those are the same questions they'd ask about any system, but AI makes them more pressing.

speaker: NORA
text: And disclosure? Do journals need to know if AI helped?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's an evolving area. In general, many journals and industry bodies have been developing guidance on AI use in writing, and a common theme is that humans remain responsible for the content and that AI use should be disclosed where relevant. I won't quote specific rules, because they vary and change. But an agency should have a clear position that it can explain to clients and authors.

speaker: NORA
text: It's interesting that Prime's chief scientific officer has been teaching on exactly this topic.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. Co-leading a session on AI in medical communications at a professional society suggests Prime wants to be part of setting good practice, not just following it. That's a credible position for a science-led agency, and it could be a selling point with cautious clients.

speaker: NORA
text: So caution makes sense.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does. But caution can become delay. The risk is that clients start expecting AI-driven efficiency, and an agency that hasn't built the capability has to either cut prices without the savings, or lose work.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the CTO's internal session on small-scale AI applications?

speaker: JAMES
text: I find that encouraging, actually. Small-scale applications, used internally, is exactly where to start. Summarising documents, checking references, drafting internal notes. Low risk, quick learning. The question is whether that turns into a systematic programme with measured outcomes.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's be specific about challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, the people-heavy model. Prime's strength is its PhD-level staff, but they're also its main cost. If revenue is tied to hours and AI reduces hours, the business model itself has to adapt.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, regulatory review slows down AI's benefit. Even if AI halves drafting time, MLR review still takes as long as it takes. So the end-to-end speed-up may be smaller than the drafting speed-up, at least until review processes adapt too. Meanwhile, faster-moving competitors could gain.

speaker: NORA
text: Third.

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, scale relative to the big groups. Larger agency networks can invest more in AI. Prime has to choose carefully, focusing on use cases that matter most to its clients.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Visibility. Little public data on scale, no named AI product, and thin news flow over the past two years. For a company in a mature private equity hold, a clearer public story would help, in my view. Not every private company needs to publish numbers, but a visible AI offer would make the positioning more credible.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration and cross-selling. The acquisitions brought in health economics, digital and US payer expertise. The value comes when those teams work together on the same clients. That's harder than it sounds in agencies, where teams often have their own cultures and client relationships.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the writers themselves? How do they feel about AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have any public information on Prime's staff views, so this is general. In many expert professions, people have mixed feelings. Some are excited to offload the tedious parts of the job. Others worry about their craft being devalued, or about their jobs. And some are simply sceptical, because they've seen AI make confident mistakes in their field.

speaker: NORA
text: And that matters for adoption.

speaker: JAMES
text: Hugely. If the writers don't trust the tools, they'll either avoid them or spend so long double-checking that there's no saving. The best approach, in my view, is to involve senior writers in designing how AI is used, let them set the quality bar, and be honest about how the role will evolve. People adopt tools they helped shape.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a career question too, for junior writers?

speaker: JAMES
text: There is, and it's one many professions face. Junior writers often learn by doing the routine work: summarising documents, building first drafts. If AI does that, how do they learn? Agencies will need to design training so that juniors still develop judgment, perhaps by reviewing and correcting AI drafts under supervision. It's a solvable problem, but it needs deliberate attention.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: The exit question. After five and a half years, a future buyer will ask what AI does to this business. If the answer is a threat with no response, that weighs on value. If the answer is a measured productivity gain plus new AI-enabled services, that supports it.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, opportunities. Where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: First, generative AI first drafts for publications, abstracts and slide kits, with MLR tracking built in. The lever is writer hours per deliverable. We don't have Prime's numbers, so we can't put a figure on it, but in a business where expert time is the main cost, even modest time savings matter.

speaker: NORA
text: But if hours fall, don't fees fall?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's why the second opportunity matters. Productise Prime Solutions Lab into named, fixed-fee evidence and insight services. Instead of selling hours, sell outcomes: a defined evidence synthesis, a landscape analysis, a predictive model of which audiences need what. When the price is fixed and AI makes delivery faster, the efficiency becomes margin rather than a discount.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-sell. Combine Aventine's US payer work with HCD's health economics, and offer both to existing pharma clients. A client using Prime for European health economics may also need US payer communications. That's not an AI opportunity directly, but AI-assisted evidence work can make the combined offer faster.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Digital tools from earthware inside the omnichannel programmes that James Karcher and David Hogben lead. For example, interactive tools for doctors that explain data, built once and used across many channels.

speaker: NORA
text: And geography?

speaker: JAMES
text: Expanding US medical writing from the Aventine base. The US is the biggest market, and Prime already has people there. And acquisitions: buying a firm with AI-enabled evidence analytics would repeat the 2022 to 2023 playbook, but with an AI focus.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the patient side? One of the five service lines is patient engagement.

speaker: JAMES
text: I think that's an underappreciated area. In general, there's growing demand for plain-language summaries of research, so that patients and the public can understand what a trial found. Writing those is a skill: simple without being misleading. AI can help produce first drafts at different reading levels and in different languages, with experts checking for accuracy and balance.

speaker: NORA
text: And insights from patients?

speaker: JAMES
text: Prime's patient engagement and insights line suggests work on understanding patients' experiences. AI can help analyse large amounts of qualitative material, like survey responses, finding themes that a team then validates. That's the kind of thing Prime Solutions Lab's language about distilling complex data might point towards, although the page doesn't say so specifically.

speaker: NORA
text: Any AI opportunity on the market access side specifically?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think so. Health economics involves reviewing large amounts of published literature, building models and writing value dossiers. AI can help screen and summarise literature much faster, with experts checking. That's an area where speed and thoroughness both matter, and where clients may pay for being first.

speaker: NORA
text: One AI bet for the next eighteen months?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Generative AI-assisted first drafts of publications and slide kits, with review tracked through MLR. It's the core billable work. The expensive resource is PhD-level writer time. And it's where clients will first expect AI to make a difference.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Why not lead with Prime Solutions Lab's predictive modelling?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Because that's newer and harder to measure. Drafting is the volume business. If Prime can show that its writers produce high-quality first drafts faster, with fewer review cycles and no loss of accuracy, that's a story every client understands. And it frees time for the higher-value strategic work.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Give me the first hundred days.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: set the rules and the baseline. Agree with a few willing clients that AI can be used on their work, under clear terms. Confirm the tools and data handling, so trial data stays secure and isn't used to train outside models. Measure the baseline: hours per deliverable type, number of review cycles, number of errors found in review.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Pilot. Pick a few deliverable types, say abstracts, posters and slide kits, which are shorter and repeatable. Writers use AI to produce a first draft from the source documents, with every number and claim linked to its source. Then the writer edits and checks. Track hours, accuracy and how reviewers respond. Everything goes through normal review; nothing is published that a human expert hasn't verified.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And sixty to a hundred?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Measure and decide. Did hours per deliverable fall? Did review cycles change? Were there any accuracy problems, and what caused them? If the results are good, extend to full manuscripts and more clients, and decide how to price, ideally moving some work to fixed fees. And publish an AI policy that clients can read, covering data, disclosure and human review.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: James Karcher's role seems designed for it. But I'd pair him with the chief scientific officer, Valerie Moss, because the writers need to trust that scientific standards come first. And with the CTO for the tools and security side. Clear single accountability, with science and technology both at the table.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: How do you measure quality, not just speed?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Really important, because speed without quality is worthless here. I'd track the number and type of corrections reviewers make on AI-assisted drafts versus traditional ones. Factual errors, especially numbers and references, should be at or below the traditional baseline, and that's non-negotiable. Then softer measures: did authors and clients rate the draft as clear and well-structured? And did the number of review rounds go down?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And if quality slips?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Stop, find out why, and fix it before scaling. One serious error in front of a client can undo months of trust. That's why I'd start with a few willing clients and shorter deliverables, where problems are easy to catch.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: What's the key design rule?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Traceability. Every number and every claim in an AI-assisted draft should be linked to its source, so the writer and reviewers can check it in seconds. An AI that writes beautifully but can't show its sources is useless in this field, or worse.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do a second walk-through. Same made-up biotech?
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: Same Northbrook Therapeutics. The paper has been accepted, and now the medical affairs team needs a slide kit, a set of forty slides its medical science liaisons can use to present the trial results to specialists in balanced, non-promotional discussions.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: And the old way?
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: A writer goes back through the paper, the clinical study report and the statistical tables. She decides which results go on which slide, designs the charts with a designer, writes speaker notes, and references every statement. Then it goes through review, and comments come back: this chart is misleading, this claim needs a reference, this slide should show the safety data more prominently. Revisions, another round. It's skilled, careful work, and it takes time.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: And with AI assistance?
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: The writer loads the accepted paper and the approved tables into a secure tool. She asks for a proposed outline of forty slides following the paper's structure. The AI suggests one, she adjusts it. Then for each slide, the AI drafts the headline and bullet text, proposes which table or figure to use, and drafts speaker notes. Crucially, every statement is linked to the exact place in the source document.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: And then she checks it.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: She checks every slide. Some are good; some need rewording because the AI emphasised the wrong thing; one has a number from the wrong subgroup, which the source link makes easy to spot and fix. She spends her time on judgment, balance and clarity, rather than copying numbers. Then a designer builds the final charts, and it goes to review.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: Does review get faster?
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly, if the reviewers can see the source links too. Instead of hunting for the reference behind each claim, they click and check. That's speculative, and it depends on the client's review systems. But it's where the bigger speed-up might eventually come from, not just the drafting.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: And what does Northbrook notice?
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: JAMES
text: Ideally, the slide kit arrives sooner, with fewer errors in the first review round, and the same or better quality. And if Prime has moved this kind of work to a fixed fee, Northbrook gets price certainty while Prime keeps the efficiency gain. Both sides win, and the doctors at the end of the chain get accurate information sooner.
chapter: A slide kit with AI, a hypothetical

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from Prime?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, put AI in someone's job title. Prime did that in October 2025. When AI is everyone's side project, it's no one's responsibility. A named leader with a clear remit is a strong start.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, in regulated work, traceability is everything. Whether it's medicine, law or finance, AI is only useful if every output can be checked against its source quickly. Design for verification, not just generation.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, rethink pricing before your customers do it for you. If you sell hours and AI reduces hours, you need a plan. Fixed-fee products, outcome-based pricing, new services. Firms that move first keep the benefit; firms that wait end up giving it away in discounts.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, acquisitions are a beginning. Prime bought health economics, digital and US payer capability. The payoff comes from combining them into offers that no single piece could deliver alone. AI can be the glue, for example in evidence work that spans HEOR and communications.

speaker: NORA
text: I'd add one: experts are the best AI users, not the victims.

speaker: JAMES
text: Great point. A PhD-level medical writer using AI well is far more valuable than either the writer alone or the AI alone. The writer knows what's right; the AI does the heavy lifting. Businesses that frame AI as a tool for their experts, rather than a replacement, tend to get better adoption and better results.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a lesson about building an in-house hub like Prime Solutions Lab?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think so. Mixing creatives, technologists, strategists and scientists in one team is a smart way to make sure AI work is grounded in real client problems, rather than technology for its own sake. The risk with hubs, in general, is that they become a showcase disconnected from day-to-day delivery. The test is whether the hub's work ends up inside ordinary projects, used by ordinary teams.

speaker: NORA
text: So the hub has to be a bridge, not an island.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. A good sign would be a named tool or method that started in the lab and is now used routinely across the business. A less good sign would be a lab that produces impressive demonstrations but no change in how the core work gets done. From the outside, we can't yet tell which way it's going, which is why it's on our watch list.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the private equity world?

speaker: JAMES
text: In a services business late in a hold, a buyer will want to see that AI has been absorbed as a productivity gain, not left as an unanswered threat. Measured results, even modest ones, tell a much better story than a strategy slide.

speaker: NORA
text: Risks. Give me the list.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disruption to the revenue model. If drafting hours fall and pricing stays per hour, revenue per deliverable falls, and some clients may bring work in-house. Two, regulatory review slowing Prime's own AI rollout while rivals move faster. Three, larger agency groups with bigger AI budgets. Four, an AI error in a medical document, which could damage trust with a client very quickly. And five, the exit timing, with the AI story not yet proven publicly.

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me more about the insourcing risk.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's our inference, but here's the logic. Today a pharma company might outsource a slide kit because its own small team doesn't have time. If AI tools make that team three times more productive, it might keep more work in-house. Agencies would then be left with the most complex, strategic and surge work. That's not necessarily bad, because that work is often higher value, but the volume of routine work could shrink.

speaker: NORA
text: So the agency needs to move up the value chain.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Strategy, evidence generation, health economics, digital experiences, and the scientific judgment that clients can't easily replicate. That's where Prime's acquisitions point, and where AI can make its experts even more valuable rather than less.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a reputational risk for the industry too?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. If AI-generated medical content becomes associated with errors, or with undisclosed use, regulators and journals may tighten rules, and clients may become more cautious. Agencies that are transparent and careful will be better placed if that happens.

speaker: NORA
text: So what should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, whether Prime names an AI tool or service, especially coming out of Prime Solutions Lab. Second, whether it announces fixed-fee or outcome-based services that suggest a shift away from hours. Third, any new acquisition, especially one with AI or analytics capability. And fourth, whether it publishes an AI policy for clients, covering data handling and human review.

speaker: NORA
text: And if none of those happen in the next year?

speaker: JAMES
text: Then Prime may still be doing good work quietly, which is very common for agencies, because so much of their work is confidential. But for a company that has put AI in a senior title and launched a hub, I'd expect some public evidence of results within a year or so. A case study with a client's permission, a named service, or even a talk at an industry event sharing what the company has learned would all count.

speaker: NORA
text: And on the industry side?

speaker: JAMES
text: How publication guidelines and pharma companies' own policies on AI evolve. That will set the pace for everyone, Prime included.

text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: JAMES
text: A medical communications and market access group, staffed by scientists, serving life-science companies.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Its scientific people. Eighty percent of scientific and editorial staff with doctorates, by its count.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: A people-heavy, hours-based model, and little public evidence of AI in the core work.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI signal?

speaker: JAMES
text: An executive vice president with AI in the title, appointed October 2025.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: AI-assisted first drafts of publications and slide kits, with every claim traceable to its source.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace medical writers?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. It will change what they spend their time on, and who wins the work.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a pharma medical affairs head should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Write down your rules for agencies using AI on your work. Clear rules speed everyone up.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautiously optimistic. The leadership is in place. Now it needs measured results.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. Prime Global is a Knutsford-based medical communications and market access group, founded in 1997 and still led by its founder, that helps life-science companies communicate the science, value and patient impact of their medicines. It sells publications, medical strategy, health economics, market access, launch support and patient engagement, with a highly qualified scientific workforce. LLCP invested in April 2021, and Prime has since added health economics, digital and US payer businesses. In October 2025 it appointed an executive with AI in his title and has launched an AI-enabled hub called Prime Solutions Lab, but there's no public evidence yet of AI embedded in its core writing work. Its best bet is AI-assisted drafting with full traceability, paired with a move from hours to fixed-fee services. The risks are pricing pressure, regulatory pace and bigger rivals.

text: That's it. And the wider lesson for any expert services firm: AI rewards the businesses that change how they price at the same time as they change how they work.
